Compound.name: a short chain fatty acid
Synonyms: SCFA // a volatile fatty acid // VFA
Comment: The term "fatty acid" was originally coined to describe aliphatic monocarboxylic acids derived from or contained in esterified form in an animal or vegetable fat, oil or wax. However, over the years the term has been expanded to refer to additional, shorter monocarboxylic acids with an aliphatic tail such as |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (but not the shorter |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: ACET|). The length of a fatty acid is determined by the length of the longest carbon chain, including the carbon of the carboxy group. Common natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons in the longest chain and can be either saturated or unsaturated. In many organisms they are often modified by branching, hydroxylation, methylation, epoxidation and other types of modifications. Inside living cells fatty acids are rarely found in free form. They are usually bound to coenzyme A or acyl-carrier proteins, or form part of |FRAME: Triacylglycerides triglycerides|, |FRAME: Phospholipids phospholipids|, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|, and |FRAME: Cholesterol-esters cholesterol esters|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, alcohols, and aldehydes, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "Ultra-long-chain fatty acids"| (ULCFA) have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain. Most of the natural fatty acids have an even number of carbon atoms, since their biosynthesis involves the addition of two-carbon-atom units. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing.

Comment: Menaquinols are the reduced form of |FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinones"|. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. Menaquinones are the most widespread respiratory quinones in biological systems Fujimoto12. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are named MK- n or DMK- n , respectively, where the n refers to the number of prenyl units present in the side chain. The most common length of the side chain in bacteria is 8, although minor amounts of MK-1 through MK-14 have been found 7022156. Many bacteria and archaea have |FRAME: Dihydromenaquinones "dehydrogenated menaquinones"|, which are named MK- n (H 2 ). The degree and location of dehydrogenation depends on the species. Some organisms have menaquinones with modifications of the head group, for example |FRAME: TAX-2302| possess both |FRAME: CPD-15875 thermoplasmaquinones| (TPQ), which contains an extra methyl group, and |FRAME: CPD-15876 methionaquinones| (MTK), which contains a methylthio group 11157962. Menaquinones are also known as vitamin K 2 . Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinone"|). Since menaquinones produced by different organisms have different tail lengths there are many variations of vitamin K 2 , usually specified based on the number of carbons in their tails, such as in Vitamin K 2 (45).

It accounts for roughly 10-20% of the phospholipid fatty acid content of skeletal muscle cells. In addition to being involved in cellular signaling as a lipid second messenger, arachidonate is also a key inflammatory intermediate and can also act as a vasodilator. Compound.name: a quinol
Synonyms: quinol // a hydroquinone // a reduced quinone
Comment: A quinol, or hydroquinone, is the fully reduced form of |FRAME: Quinones|. Quinones are organic compounds derived from aromatic compounds, with two carbonyl groups incorporated into the ring structure with rearrangement of the double bonds where necessary. Quinones are conjugated but not aromatic. A classic example of a quinone is |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE|. Quinones are commonly named with a prefix that indicates the parent aromatic hydrocarbon (for example, "benzo-" for benzene, "naphtho-" for naphthalene, and "anthra-" for anthracene) with a "-quinone" suffix. Several types of quinones serve as electron acceptors in electron transport chains. Those quinones are usually prenylated with a lipid-soluble isoprenyl tail that anchors them in the membrane lipid bilayer. Quinones can carry two electrons, and when fully reduced they are referred to as |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinols|. The addition of a single H atom to a quinone results in formation of a free radical called |FRAME: Semiquinones|. Many quinone derivatives often have other biological activities, such as |FRAME: CPD-11501 "vitamin K"|.

Compound.name: starch
Comment: Starch is a glucose-based polysaccharide produced by plants, green algae, and cyanobacteria. Starch combines two polymeric carbohydrates (polysaccharides) called |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses "alpha-amylose"| and |FRAME: CPD-7043|. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses "alpha-Amylose"| contains up to several thousand alpha-glucosyl units linked almost exclusively in linear alpha(1->4) linkages, with very few branches of alpha(1->6) linkages. In |FRAME: CPD-7043|, on the other hand, branching is common, and occurs approximately every 24-30 glucose monomer units. Amylopectin is one of (if not the) largest biological polymer known and contains from 10 5 –10 6 glucose residues 9730163. Unlike |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen| molecules, which is limited to ~55,000 glucose units, the starch branched structure leads to clusters of chains that allow for indefinite growth of the polysaccharide. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses "alpha-Amylose"| accounts for 30% of starch, while |FRAME: CPD-7043| accounts for the other 70%. The dense packing of branches at the root of the clusters generates tightly packed glucan chains that are close enough to align and form parallel double helical structures. The helices within a single cluster and neighbouring clusters align and form sections of crystalline structures separated by sections of amorphous material (containing the branches) thereby generating the semi-crystalline nature of amylopectin and of the ensuing starch granule. The crystallized chains become insoluble and typically collapse into a macrogranular solid that is osmotically inert 9730163. The enzymes of starch synthesis and mobilization are unable to interact directly with the solid structure, with the exception of |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.242 "granule-bound starch synthase"| 14502990. The solid semi-crystalline starch and hydrosoluble |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen| define two distinct physical states of the same type of storage polysaccharide. Glycogen is by far the most widespread form of storage, as it is found in Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukaryotes. The appearance of semi-crystalline storage polysaccharides appears linked to the requirement of unicellular diazotrophic cyanobacteria to fuel nitrogenase and protect it from oxygen through respiration of large amounts of stored carbon 21220783.

Compound.name: NAD(P) +
Comment: |FRAME: NAD-P-OR-NOP| is a class of compounds including the instances |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP|. |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| are dinucleotides containing one |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| base and one |FRAME: ADENINE| base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety. These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). They are often referred to as coenzymes, although in most of their reactions they function as cosubstrates rather than true coenzymes. The most common function of |FRAME: NAD| is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts |FRAME: NAD| to |FRAME: NADH|, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form. |FRAME: NADPH|, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of |FRAME: NADP|, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms |FRAME: NADP| is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-84|. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY|).

Compound.name: a modified amino acid within a protein

Comment: Mycolic acids are the hallmark of the cell envelope of |FRAME: TAX-1773| and related species and genera. They comprise a homologous series of C60-C90 (2 R )-alkyl-(3 R )-hydroxy very long-chain fatty acids, and are found as either esters of |FRAME: Arabinogalactan| or as free lipids in the form of trehalose dimycolate (TDM). Both forms contribute to forming the two leaflets of the mycobacterial outer membrane, also called the mycomembrane, which protects the organism from antibiotics and the host's immune system |CITS: [15653820][17555433][15353567]|. There is a significant variability in the structure of mycolic acids among different species. Acids from |FRAME: TAX-1716| species contain 22-38 carbon atoms, |FRAME: TAX-697025| and |FRAME: TAX-697025| spp. contain 30-36, |FRAME: TAX-37914| spp. contain 34-38, |FRAME: TAX-1827| spp. contain 34-52 in, |FRAME: TAX-1817| spp. contain 46-60, |FRAME: TAX-2053 Gordonia | spp. contain 46-66, |FRAME: TAX-2060| spp. contain 64-78 , |FRAME: TAX-1763| spp. contain 60-90, and |FRAME: TAX-286801| spp. contain up to 100 carbon atoms 24374164. The acids are formed by a Claisen-type condensation of two components - the meromycolic chain and a fatty acid. The meromycolic chain of |FRAME: TAX-1773| typically incorporates a hydroxy group at C-1, a cyclopropyl ring fused onto the C-16/C-17 bond (at either a cis or a trans configuration), a methoxyl or oxo group at C-35, and a methyl group at C-36. The modifications and their positions may change among strains and species. Several structural classes of mycolic acids exist. In |FRAME: TAX-1773| the most apolar ones, known as alpha-mycolic acids, contain 74-80 carbon atoms (out of which 22-26 carbons are located in the fatty acid moiety and the rest on the mero-chain) and generally two double bonds (that can be in either cis - or trans -configuration) or two cis -cyclopropyl groups located in the meromycolic chain. The cyclopropane rings are believed to protect the organism from oxidative stress 15653820. alpha-Mycolic acids usually comprise more than 70 percent of the total mycolic acids in the cell. Other classes are defined by additional oxygen functions located in the distal part of the meromycolic chain, and include keto-, methoxy-, wax ester-, epoxy-, and hydroxy-types. In |FRAME: TAX-1773| the oxygenated mycolic acids (keto-, methoxy-, and hydroxy-types) contain ~84-88 carbon atoms, and are thus four to six carbons longer than the alpha-mycolic acids from the same strains. The biosynthesis of mycolic acids is described in |FRAME: PWYG-321|.

The functional group of lipoate is a ditholane ring, which is a cyclic disulfide. The enzyme complexes that require lipoate have a dedicated |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein "lipoyl domain"|, and lipoate is actually produced on this domain. The precursor |FRAME: CPD-195| molecule is first attached to a specific |FRAME: LYS| residue within the lipoyl domain (producing |FRAME: Octanoylated-domains|), and is then converted to lipoate by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-782|, resulting in |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein-N6-lipoyllysine|. |FRAME: CPLX0-782 "Lipoate synthase"| not only catalyzes the reaction, but is also the source of the two sulfur atoms.

Compound.name: a carotenoid
Comment: |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A. Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see 15012246). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis. Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Although biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis from |FRAME: CPD1F-114| have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated, details of all of the enzyme reactions involved in these pathways remain to be determined (as in |CITS: [20802040] [17008032] [11511870] [11432736]|). Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|. Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses 20582313.

Compound.name: a K vitamin
Comment: Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones|). Since menaquinones produced by different organisms have different tail lenghts, there are many variations of vitamin K 2 , usually specified based on the number of carbons in their tails, such as in Vitamin K 2 (45). Menaquinones are synthesized by gut bacteria, and are absorbed into the blood. Thus, dietary deficiency is extremely rare in healthy individuals. There are also several synthetic forms- vitamin K 3 through K 9 . Vitamin K 3 (|FRAME: CPD-3766|) is the most active of the synthetic forms.

Compound.name: a reduced flavin
Comment: A |FRAME: FLAVIN flavin| is a chemical moiety found in the compounds |FRAME: FAD| and |FRAME: FMN|, both important redox cofactors involved in many important reactions in metabolism. Flavin can exist in two different redox states, which it converts between by accepting or donating electrons. The |FRAME: Oxidized-Flavins "fully oxidized form"| (or quinone form) accepts two electrons and two protons to become the |FRAME: Reduced-Flavins "fully reduced form"| (hydroquinone form). The reduced form can be oxidized to a semireduced form (semiquinone) by donating one electron and one proton. A second oxidation results in restoring the initial quinone form. The conjugated ring system of fully oxidized flavin confers a bright yellow color, and its name is derived from flavus , Latin for yellow. Flavins are synthesized from |FRAME: GTP| in the form of |FRAME: RIBOFLAVIN|, which is later modified into |FRAME: FMN| or |FRAME: FAD|. Since mammals cannot synthesize |FRAME: RIBOFLAVIN|, it is an essential vitamin for them.

Compound.name: a siderophore-bound Fe(III)
Synonyms: an iron(III) chelate // an Fe 3+ -siderophore // a ferric-siderophore complex
Comment: This entry stands for siderophores-bound |FRAME: FE+3| cation(s). Siderophores are small, high-affinity iron chelating compounds secreted by microorganisms. Once outside the cell, siderophores bind |FRAME: FE+3| with high affinity, and the iron-siderophore complexes are imported back into the cell by active-transport mechanisms. Siderophores are very common in pathogenic bacteria, since iron in the host organism is usually tightly bound to proteins, resulting in an extremely low concentration of free iron in the blood. Most siderophores belong to one of three major groups: the |FRAME: Catecholate-siderophores "catechols"|, |FRAME: Hydroxamate-siderophores "hydroxamates"| and |FRAME: Thiazoline-siderophores "thiazolines"|. Some grasses are known to make siderophores as well. These |FRAME: Phytosiderophores "phytosiderophores"| are also known as mugineic acids.

The most relevant anteiso-fatty acids in food and bacteria are |FRAME: CPD-9917| and |FRAME: CPD-23509| 28129363. Unlike classic fatty acids and |FRAME: Iso-fatty-acids " iso -fatty acids"|, anteiso -fatty acids are chiral molecules due to the stereogenic center at the carbon of the branching point. A distinct pre-dominance of ( S )- anteiso -fatty acids, or even ( S )-enantiopurity has been described in bacteria |CITS: [1886522][20117788]|, and also in fish |CITS: [13373794][17508720][20221853]|, dairy products |CITS: [13373794][13412644][13827622][20221853]|, mutton fat 13018208, and Brussel sprouts 26390192.

Compound.name: a long-chain fatty acid
Comment: The term "fatty acid" was originally coined to describe aliphatic monocarboxylic acids derived from or contained in esterified form in an animal or vegetable fat, oil or wax. However, over the years the term has been expanded to refer to additional, shorter monocarboxylic acids with an aliphatic tail such as |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (but not the shorter |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: ACET|). The length of a fatty acid is determined by the length of the longest carbon chain, including the carbon of the carboxy group. Common natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons in the longest chain and can be either saturated or unsaturated. In many organisms they are often modified by branching, hydroxylation, methylation, epoxidation and other types of modifications. Inside living cells fatty acids are rarely found in free form. They are usually bound to coenzyme A or acyl-carrier proteins, or form part of |FRAME: Triacylglycerides triglycerides|, |FRAME: Phospholipids phospholipids|, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|, and |FRAME: Cholesterol-esters cholesterol esters|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, alcohols, and aldehydes, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "Ultra-long-chain fatty acids"| (ULCFA) have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain. Most of the natural fatty acids have an even number of carbon atoms, since their biosynthesis involves the addition of two-carbon-atom units. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing.

Compound.name: a methanofuran
Comment: Methanofurans are a group of related carbon-carrier cofactors involved in the first step of the methanogenic reduction of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|). Methanofurans react with |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| to form the carbamate N -carboxymethanofuran, which is reduced to |FRAME: Formyl-methanofurans| by |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.12|. In addition, the cofactor also participates at a later stage of all methanogenesis pathways. These pathways converge at the compound Me-CoM, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|; the latter process involves methanofuran (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|). Methanofuran is also used by methylotrophic bacteria as a coenzyme to oxidize formaldehyde to formate |CITS: [9651254][11532013]|. Fucosyl residues are typically absent from seed xyloglucans but present on the xyloglucans in the vegatative portions of the same plant Mishra09. Most xylosylglucans consist of repeating heptasaccharide |FRAME: Xyloglucans-Xylose XXXG| units. The average molecular weight of xyloglucan is more than 50,000 Mishra09. Comment: The histo-blood group antigen precursor disaccharides are found at the terminal end of oligosaccharide chains attached to proteins or sphingolipids, and serve as the actual substrates for various glycosyltransferases that terminate the chain elongation process, forming the ABH or Lewis antigens. Five types of precursor disaccharides are known to carry ABH activity - type 1 through type 4 and type 6. Type 1 precursors are widely expressed on endodermally-derived tissues such as lining epithelia and glandular epithelia. Type 2 precursors are found mainly on ecto- or mesodermally-derived tissues, including erythrocytes Mollicone86. Type 3 and 4 precursors are found on ecto- or endodermally-derived tissues, including the salivary glands and kidneys 2464874. Since ABH antigens are present not only on erythrocytes, but also on various organs such as the salivary glands and kidneys |CITS: [3965299][6172274]|, they are called histo-blood group ABH antigens. Note the the type 3 histo-blood group antigen precursor disaccharide corresponds to the |FRAME: Core1 "O-glycan core 1 "| structure. Six types of precursor disaccharides have been described: |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R|: beta-D-galactosyl-(1->3)- N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-R |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R|: beta-D-galactosyl-(1->4)- N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-R |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-alpha-GalNac-R|: beta-D-galactosyl-(1->3)- N -acetyl-alpha-D-galactosaminyl-R |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GalNac-R|: beta-D-galactosyl-(1->3)- N -acetyl-beta-D-galactosaminyl-R |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-Gal-R|: beta-D-galactosyl-(1,3)-beta-D-galactosyl-R |FRAME: beta-Gal-14-beta-Glc-R|: beta-D-galactosyl-(1,4)-beta-D-glucosyl-R

Compound.name: a pectate
Synonyms: poly(1,4-alpha-D-galacturonate)(n) // (1,4-alpha-D-D-galactosyluronate)n // 1,4-alpha-D-galacturonide // a pectic acid // an alpha-D-polygalacturonic acid // a poly(1,4-alpha-D-galacturonate)
Comment: |FRAME: Pectin "Pectin"| is a structural heteropolysaccharide consisting of a complex set of polysaccharides that is present in most primary cell walls and is particularly abundant in the non-woody parts of terrestrial plants. It s involved in crosslinking cellulose and hemicellulose fibers, which provides rigidity to the cell wall. The characteristic structure of pectin is a linear chain of alpha-(1-4)-linked |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| that forms the pectin-backbone, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl|. Different components of pectin have different substitutions and additions. A common type is |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan I"| (RG-I), which makes up 20-35% of pectin. In RG-I some of the |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| units in the backbone are replaced by (1-2)-linked |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, to which side chains of various neutral sugars branch off, mostly |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-25028|. Another common type is |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan II"| (RG-II), which makes up about 10% of pectin. RG-II is based on a backbone of 8-9 galacturonate units, which are decorated by four side chains consisting of 12 different types of sugars in more than 20 different linkages. RG-II usually forms dimeric structures via the formation of crosslinks by a 1:2 borate diol ester between apiosyl residues in one of the side chains. Other types of pectin include chains of apiogalacturonan, homogalacturonan, and xylogalacturonan. There is currently no consensus as to how the pectic polysaccharides are linked to each other, or to other polymers, in the wall. However, it is thought that the different peptides are covalently linked to each other via their backbones, forming a large linear structure with many side branches |CITS: [11423143][12162553][Coenen07]|. In nature, around 80% of the carboxyl groups of the galacturonate units are esterified with |FRAME: METOH|. Some plants, including sugar beet, potatoes and pears, contain pectins with acetylated galacturonate in addition to methyl esters. Partially esterified pectins are often referred to as pectinate, and if the degree of esterification is below 5%, |FRAME: PECTATE|.

Comment: The |FRAME: Gaburedins gaburedins| are a family of gamma-aminobutanoate (GABA)-derived ureas whose biosynthesis is encoded by a silent gene cluster in the |FRAME: TAX-54571| genome. The cluster, which consists of the three genes |FRAME: G-124751|, |FRAME: G-124752|, and gbnC , is located adjacent to a putative regulatory system homologous to the the mmfR - mmfLHP - mmyR cluster of |FRAME: TAX-100226|. The products of the mmfLHP genes are the |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, which act as inducers of |FRAME: CPD-27200 methylenomycin| production in |FRAME: TAX-100226|, while MmfR and MmyR are ArpA-like transcriptional repressors, which repress |FRAME: CPD-27200 methylenomycin| production 18988741. Based on the sequence homology, it was hypothesized that the gbnABC genes encode a natural product(s), whose production is controlled by a regulatory system encoded by the mmfR - mmfLHP - mmyR genes homologs. The gbn cluster contains highly conserved DNA sequence, which were predicted to be binding motifs for the transcriptional repressor GbnR, the mmyR homolog. To test this hypothesis, the gbnR gene was knocked out. Indeed, the mutant produced six new metabolites, the products of the gbnABC genes, which were named gaburedin A-F. The compounds structures were shown to be gamma-aminobutanoate (GABA)-derived ureas, containing an amino acid linked by a ureido bridge Sidda14.

Common cellodextrins are cellotriose, cellotetraose, cellopentaose and cellohexaose.

The nucleosides are called |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| when the sugar is |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose|, and |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| when it is |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|. Common |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| include |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, |FRAME: URIDINE|, |FRAME: ADENOSINE|, |FRAME: GUANOSINE| and |FRAME: INOSINE|. Examples of |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| include |FRAME: THYMIDINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYADENOSINE|. When nucleosides are phosphorylated on the sugar's primary alcohol group, the resulting phosphonucleosides are called |FRAME: Nucleotides nucleotides|. Pyrimidine is a heterocyclic aromatic compound similar to benzene, containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 of the ring. The name pyrimidines is also used for compounds derived from the basic pyrimidine compound, including three of the nucleosides found in nucleic acids, namely |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, THYMIDINE, and |FRAME: URIDINE|.

Compound.name: candicidin
Comment: Candicidin is an aromatic polyene macrolide antibiotic produced by some species of |FRAME: TAX-1883|. It has a complex structure composed of a macrolide ring, the amino sugar |FRAME: CPD-16768|, and an aromatic moiety, |FRAME: CPD-16769|. Lechevalier first described this antibiotic as C135 and it was renamed candicidin due to its strong action against |FRAME: TAX-5475 Candida | species including one of the most common human fungal pathogens |FRAME: TAX-5476| 13159187. The increased susceptibility of immunocompromised patients to fungal attacks has stimulated research efforts to isolate effective antifungal agents (reviewed in |CITS: [19362642][12664141]|). The same compound was isolated independently from |FRAME: TAX-206662|, and named FR-008. Despite initial reports that FR-008 is different from candicidin, it was later shown that the two compounds are in fact identical 18559273. Structural elucidation of candicidin revealed that it consists of three components named |FRAME: CPD-13108|, |FRAME: CPD-17190|, and |FRAME: CPD-17191|. Compound.name: an anthracycline
Comment: Anthracyclines are a class of antibiotics produced by |FRAME: TAX-1883| bacteria that are used in cancer as chemotherapy drugs. This group of antibiotics is defined by the presence of a four fused-ring aromatic system, based on a 7,8,9,10-tetrahydro-5,12-naphthacenequinone framework, which usually occurs as a glycoside with a deoxy(amino)sugar. The framework is synthesized by a polyketide-synthase from an acetyl-CoA or propanoyl-CoA starter unit and malonyl-CoA extender units, and subsequently modified by other enzymes 11851469. The anthracyclines intercalate between base pairs of the DNA/RNA strand, inhibit topoisomerase II enzymes, and prevent DNA replication. They are among the most effective anticancer treatments ever developed and are effective against more types of cancer than any other class of chemotherapeutic agents.

Compound.name: a menaquinone
Comment: Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. Menaquinones are the most widespread respiratory quinones in biological systems Fujimoto12. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are named MK- n or DMK- n , respectively, where the n refers to the number of prenyl units present in the side chain. The most common length of the side chain in bacteria is 8, although minor amounts of MK-1 through MK-14 have been found 7022156. Many bacteria and archaea have |FRAME: Dihydromenaquinones "dehydrogenated menaquinones"|, which are named MK- n (H 2 ). The degree and location of dehydrogenation depends on the species. Some organisms have menaquinones with modifications of the head group, for example |FRAME: TAX-2302| possess both |FRAME: CPD-15875 thermoplasmaquinones| (TPQ), which contains an extra methyl group, and |FRAME: CPD-15876 methionaquinones| (MTK), which contains a methylthio group 11157962. Menaquinones are also known as vitamin K 2 . Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinone"|). Since menaquinones produced by different organisms have different tail lengths there are many variations of vitamin K 2 , usually specified based on the number of carbons in their tails, such as in Vitamin K 2 (45). The reduced form of menaquinone is called |FRAME: Menaquinols|.

Compound.name: a jasmonate or derivative
Comment: The |FRAME: Jasmonates jasmonates| are a group of important phytohormones, structurally similar to animal |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins| and ubiquitous in the plant kingdom. Many forms exist, based on the structure of |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "Jasmonate"| (jasmonic acid, JA). The jasmonates act as regulatory molecules in many developmental processes that include fertility, sex determination, root elongation and fruit ripening. They are also potent signals activating plant defences against pathogens, herbivory, wounding and abiotic stress. The jasmonate regulation system includes the COI1 receptor protein and several JAZ ( JA smonate Z IM domain) repressors, which, in the absence of jasmonate, are bound to the MYC2 transcription factors, preventing transcription. In the presence of active jasmonate molecules, COI1 interacts with the JAZ repressors, causing their |FRAME: PWY-7511 ubiquitylation|. The ubiquitylated repressors are targeted for proteasome degradation, releasing the MYC2 transcription factors and activating transcription 19716757. Only two of the four stereoisomers of jasmonate occur naturally: |FRAME: CPD-731| and |FRAME: CPD-734| |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. These two forms are present in equilibrium within cells and can interconvert spontaneously through epimerization |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. The exact ratio of these stereoisomers within a cell has not been conclusively determined, and it may vary based on species, cell type, and physiological state. But, in the systems tested so far, |FRAME: CPD-734| is found at higher levels than |FRAME: CPD-731| 19349968. The biological activity of these stereoisomers can be quite different 8074303. In addition, enzymes involved in JA metabolism may have different preferences for the different stereoisomers 17291501. This master class includes a large set of cyclopentanone derivatives of |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "jasmonate"|. Confusingly, these compounds are often referred to collectively by the name "jasmonates".

Compound.name: a 2-demethylmenaquinol
Comment: Menaquinols are the reduced form of |FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinones"|. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are named MK- n or DMK- n , respectively, where the n refers to the number of prenyl units present in the side chain. The most common length of the side chain in bacteria is 8, although minor amounts of MK-1 through MK-14 have been found 7022156. Menaquinones are also known as vitamin K 2 . Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinone"|). Since menaquinones produced by different organisms have different tail lenghts there are many variations of vitamin K 2 , usually specified based on the number of carbons in their tails, such as in Vitamin K 2 (45).

Compound.name: a furanocoumarin
Comment: The |FRAME: Furanocoumarins furanocoumarins| are one of the main groups of coumarins. Their synthesis starts with the coupling of |FRAME: CPD-4211| to the coumarin |FRAME: CPD-8186|, leading to formation of a skeleton that contains a furan ring fused with coumarin. Furanocoumarins are minor constituents in plants belonging to |FRAME: TAX-4037|, |FRAME: TAX-3803|, |FRAME: TAX-3487|, and |FRAME: TAX-23513| families. They are natural toxins that protect the plants from insects, herbivory, and microbes. Production is triggered by several types of stresses, including fungal infections |CITS: [6682038][8062387]| and stresses such as wounding Zangerl90 or acid fog Dercks90 . Furanocoumarins are also toxic to humans. Direct contact with the sap from some plants containing furanocoumarins (such as |FRAME: TAX-380077|) causes inflammation, burns and irritating sensitivity to sunlight 33174568. Some naturally occurring methoxy derivatives of furanocoumarins have been applied clinically, coupled with exposure to sunlight, to cure dermatological diseases for more than 2000 years. Linear furanocoumarins such as |FRAME: CPD-13042| and |FRAME: 5-METHOXYFURANOCOUMARIN| are used in the clinic in combination with UV radiation to treat several diseases, such as mycosis fungoides, vitiligo and psoriasis. Several clinical trials are ongoing to evaluate furanocoumarins potential to treat additional conditions, such as graft versus host disease, Crohn's disease, and several cancer types 33174568. A well documented toxicity of furanocoumarins is related to their inhibition of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes 14769198. An example is the interaction of furanocoumarins produced by grapefruit with |FRAME: HS08544-MONOMER| (CYP3A4), an enzyme that is involved in the bioinactivation of about 50% of all drugs currently used, resulting in enhanced systemic drug concentration through impaired drug metabolism, and leading to recommendation to avoid grapefruit while taking drugs 23184849.

Based on their structure, nucleobases are divided into |FRAME: Purines purines| and |FRAME: Pyrimidine-Bases pyrimidines|. |FRAME: PYRIMIDINE-RING Pyrimidine| is a heterocyclic aromatic compound similar to benzene, containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 of the ring. The name pyrimidines is also used for compounds derived from the basic pyrimidine compound, including three of the bases found in nucleic acids, namely |FRAME: CYTOSINE|, THYMINE, and |FRAME: URACIL|.

The |FRAME: FORSSMAN-HAPTEN "Forssman hapten"| (Fs), which was described in 1911 Forssman11, is one of the most potent haptenic sphingoglycolipids |CITS: [13239189][14241772][4538505][4199759][4459265]|. However, some individuals with the enigmatic ABO subgroup A pae were shown to expressed Fs glycolipids on their erythrocites 23255552. The compound was also reported from human tumors 4634984. Primates and humans have a gene that encodes the Fs synthase, but it encodes an inactive protein 10506200. It is also a key metabolite for many bacterial and archaeal species. Depending on the physiological conditions, formate serves various roles, such as to act as a reductant in anaerobic respiration, be oxidized aerobically, be secreted, or be converted to hydrogen and CO 2 . Formate is particularly common in anaerobic habitats, produced as a fermentation product of some species and used as a growth substrate for others. It is crucial compound in many syntrophic associations, in which organisms live close to the thermodynamic limit (for example, sulfate-reducing bacteria and methanogens) |CITS: [18708519][20844539]|. Its redox potential is low (around -420 mV), which allows it to donate an electron for the reduction of fumarate. In eukaryotes formate is produced from a variety of nutrients, and can be fed into a number of biosynthetic pathways. A common source of formate is the catabolism of serine or glycine (via tetrahydrofolate). Another important source is formaldehyde, which is formed by many demethylation enzymes and as a degradation product of methanol. Formate is also produced during sterol synthesis, polyamine synthesis, and tryptophan degradation, and is used during purine synthesis, thymidylate synthesis, and as the source of carbon for methylation reactions via folate and methionine (formate can be assimilated into folate by |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.3| and its carbon transferred to methionine by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13|. Comment: General Background |FRAME: CPD-22925 Spectinomycin| is an aminoglycoside antibiotic produced by |FRAME: TAX-68270| and related species. It has a unique tricyclic structure in which a single sugar component, |FRAME: CPD-27051|, is linked to the diaminocyclitol moiety (|FRAME: CPD-27044|) by beta-glycosidic and hemiketal bonds. |FRAME: CPD-22925 Spectinomycin| possesses a broad spectrum of activities against many Gram-positive as well as Gram-negative bacteria 4274968. It binds to the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome, inhibiting the binding of the elongation factor G and interrupting protein synthesis. It possesses a particularly potent activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and is used (as its dihydrochloride pentahydrate) to treat gonorrhea in cases where the organism has acquired resistance to penicillin 14461632. Spectinomycin was discovered in 1961 under the name actinospectacin |CITS: [13767811][13711223][13761690][13867836]| and later sold under the trade name Trobicin (among others). It is included in the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines.

Compound.name: biotin
Synonyms: vitamin H // coenzyme R // D-biotin // vitamin B 7
Comment: |FRAME: BIOTIN "Biotin"| is a water soluble, heterocyclic cofactor for a small number of enzymes that facilitate the transfer of CO 2 during carboxylation, decarboxylation and transcarboxylation reactions involved in fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism |CITS: [SHELLHAMMER90][11706201][15012185]|. The biotin-requiring enzymes identified so far (including |FRAME: ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLMULTI-CPLX|, |FRAME: CPLX66-17|, |FRAME: CPLX-5203|, and |FRAME: CPLX-6001|) play essential roles in cell metabolism 8676868. Humans and other mammals cannot synthesize biotin and thus must obtain it from exogenous sources via intestinal absorption. Biotin was first discovered at the turn of the 20th century as a yeast growth factor, and was named bios Wildiers01. 30 years later, the compound was purified from egg yolk by Koegl and Toennis Koegl36. In a completely unrelated research, Gyoergy and his colleagues discovered biotin in liver in 1931, and isolated it in 1941. They named it vitamin H (for the German word for skin: Haut) Vigneaud41. At the same time, another group, which was working on Rhizobia bacteria, also identified it as an essential cofactor, which they named coenzyme R Allison38. Already in 1933, Gyoergy suggested that coenzyme R, bios and vitamin H were all the same molecule. The structure of biotin was solved in 1941 -1942 |CITS: [Vigneaud41B][Melville42]|. In 1949 the first evidence was published demonstrating the biochemical role of biotin in carboxylation reactions, Lardy49, and in 1958 it was suggested that biotin was probably associated with an enzyme 13560478. Shortly after this finding, Lynen et al Lynen61 described biotin's biological function as a cofactor in the biotin-dependent carboxylases. (This historical background is adapted from 12658511).

It accounts for roughly 10-20% of the phospholipid fatty acid content of skeletal muscle cells. Compound.name: isoprene
Comment: Isoprene is a volatile compound produced by many plants. The yearly production of isoprene emissions by vegetation is around 600 million tonnes (with half of it coming from tropical broadleaf trees), making it about a third of all hydrocarbons released into the atmosphere Guenther06. Isoprene is incorporated into cell membranes in response to heat stress, and its stabilizing effect confers some tolerance to heat spikes. Its emission increases dramatically with temperature and maximizes at around 40 °C. Thus, it is thought that isoprene protects plants against heat stress 17921528. It also confers some resistance to reactive oxygen species 19183288. Isoprene is a common structural motif in biological polymers, although those compounds (|FRAME: Polyisoprenoids isoprenoids|) are not derived from isoprene, but instead are synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-4211| and its isomer |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|. Isoprene is used to produce a diverse range of industrial products including a wide variety of specialty elastomers used in surgical gloves, motor mounts and fittings, rubber bands, golf balls, and shoes. It is also used as a component of Styrene-isoprene-styrene block copolymers that form an essential part of most hot-melt pressure-sensitive adhesive formulations, and of cis -polyisoprene or synthetic rubber, which is used in tire manufacturing Whited2010.

It contains a contracted porphinoid ring with a cobalt ion ligated at its center, and further held in place by a lower axial base (a dimethylbenzimidazole) and an upper methyl or (as in this case) adenosyl group. Compound.name: Mg 2+
Synonyms: magnesium // magnesium(II) // Mg ++ // magnesium ion // Mg II
Comment: Many hundreds of enzymes require magnesium ions (Mg 2+ ) for their catalytic action, including all enzymes using or synthesizing ATP and those that use other nucleotides to synthesize DNA and RNA. The interaction between magnesium ions and phosphate makes magnesium essential to basic nucleic acid chemistry, and the common ATP molecule is normally found in a chelate with a magnesium ion. Photosynthetic organisms require Mg for the biosynthesis of chlorophyll, which is essential for photosynthesis. The function of magnesium in the center of the porphyrin ring in chlorophyll is similar to that of iron in the center of the porphyrin ring in heme. Mg is the fourth-most abundant element in the human body (Ca 2+ > K + > Na + > Mg 2+ ).

Compound.name: NADH
Synonyms: NADH 2 // NADH2 // dihydrodiphosphopyridine nucleotide // diphosphopyridine nucleotide reduced // dihydronicotinamide adenine dinucleotide // nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide reduced // NAD-reduced // NADH+H+ // DPNH // beta-NADH // beta-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, reduced
Comment: |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| are dinucleotides containing one |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| base and one |FRAME: ADENINE| base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety. These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as |FRAME: Cofactors cofactors|. They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes". The most common function of |FRAME: NAD| is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts |FRAME: NAD| to |FRAME: NADH|, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form. |FRAME: NADPH|, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of |FRAME: NADP|, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms |FRAME: NADP| is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-84|. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY|).

The reduced form can be oxidized to a |FRAME: FADH "semireduced form"| (semiquinone, FADH) by donating one electron and one proton. The semiquinone is then oxidized back to the fully oxidized form by losing a second electron and proton. Even though FAD has an aromatic ring system, FADH2 does not, making it significantly higher in energy. Many proteins contain a flavin moiety, either in the form of FAD or |FRAME: FMN|. They are known as |FRAME: Flavoproteins flavoproteins|.

Comment: Selenium is an essential trace element that is crucial for the normal development of bacteria and animals. High concentrations of selenium are however toxic, largely because transporters and enzymes involved in sulfur and sulfo-compound metabolism can often erroneously substitute |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for sulfur and can misincorporate seleno-amino acids into proteins 21913064. In humans the safety threshold between acute selenium poisoning (>400 mug/day) and selenium deficiency (<40 mug/day) is very narrow. The natural forms of selenium include |FRAME: SELENATE| [Se(VI)], |FRAME: SELENITE| [Se(IV)], |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| [Se(0)], and |FRAME: SE-2| [Se(-II)]. Selenite is the most toxic, while elemental selenium is insoluble and is generally considered to be non-toxic 25631289. However, selenium rarely occurs in its elemental state in nature. Elemental selenium can be formed by certain organisms, usually by reduction of the oxidized forms |FRAME: SELENATE| and |FRAME: SELENITE|. Some bacterial species are known to form selenium nanoparticles that consist of elemental selenium coated by a mixture of proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates |CITS: [26801915][32854560][35398797]|.
